items.body:
TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index was down more than 350 points in late-morning trading amid losses in the base metal and technology sectors, while U.S. stock markets also moved lower.

The S&P/TSX composite index was down 363.80 points at 35,620.18.

In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 18.35 points at 51,651.75. The S&P 500 index was down 60.72 points at 7,744.73, while the Nasdaq composite was down 286.36 points at 26,918.02.

The Canadian dollar traded for 70.02 cents US compared with 70.31 cents US on Tuesday.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

items.title: Trump says oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is set to begin. It’s not that simple

items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump said that “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in “our new and beautiful Greenland,” though it wasn’t clear what developments he was referring to on an island where resource extraction has stymied companies for decades.
items.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said that “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in “our new and beautiful Greenland,” though it wasn’t clear what developments he was referring to on an island where resource extraction has stymied companies for decades.

Despite Trump’s optimism, the harsh climate of Greenland -- a self-governing territory of Denmark, rather than a part of the United States -- as well as a lack of infrastructure have foiled all previous attempts to extract so-called rare earth minerals, as well as oil and gas. No efforts have ever progressed beyond the exploratory stage, and a moratorium on new gas and oil permits has been in place for several years.

“Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform following a campaign event Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska.

Trump was stumping for Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is seeking a third term to represent the state in an election against Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola.

Rising energy prices -- a direct result of the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28 after the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes -- are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for working class Americans before the midterm elections next month. Trump’s comments are likely aimed at addressing voters’ concerns before Election Day on Nov. 3.

Recent deal paved way for more U.S. bases but no exploration rights

Last month, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, following months of tensions with NATO allies over the U.S. president’s repeated demands to take control of the semiautonomous Danish territory. It doesn’t grant the U.S. any special exploration rights, but does place some limits on investments by non-NATO countries in strategic sectors.

The deal also paved the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eased tensions over Trump’s repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States. The agreement would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.

Trump has expressed his desire to acquire Greenland since 2019 and, during his second term, issued threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a NATO ally.

Naaja H. Nathanielsen, who represents Greenland in Denmark’s parliament, told The Associated Press on Wednesday that she wasn’t very surprised -- or concerned -- following Trump’s post.

“This is just the way the president decides to engage,” she said. “I think we have all come to expect something like that.”

Nathanielsen said that any current projects regarding resource extraction were still years away from potential success. She said that she believes Americans worried about the price of gas were the post’s intended audience, rather than Greenlanders, before the upcoming election.

“I recognize the worry in the U.S., but I think it’s not a quick fix,” she told the AP. “There’s no Greenlandic barrels of oil on ground in any near future.”

Nathanielsen also said that she wasn’t upset by Trump calling the island “our Greenland.”

“I think, of course, it’s somewhat disrespectful,” she said. “But you can also see it as a term of endearment if you wanted to be very generous. Right now, I don’t think much of it.”

Representatives from Denmark’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as from Greenland’s prime minister and the island’s mining ministry, did not immediately return requests for comment Wednesday.

Greenland has valuable resources

Greenland has large deposits of the rare earth minerals that are needed to make everything from computers and smartphones to the batteries, solar and wind technologies that will power the transition away from fossil fuels. China currently dominates the world’s supply of these critical minerals and the Trump administration is seeking to break Beijing’s chokehold on them.

The U.S. Geological Survey has also identified major potential offshore deposits of oil and natural gas.

But tapping these resources could be prohibitively difficult: The rare earth minerals are encased in rock, and the offshore oil and natural gas deposits are covered by Arctic ice. And in 2021, Greenlandic lawmakers said the island would not issue any new oil and gas permits because of the environmental impacts of oil extraction, and a desire to avoid further worsening of the global climate crisis.

Trump boasts about Greenland’s strategic spot in the Arctic

Trump’s Truth Social post also touted Greenland’s strategic location, saying that “from a Security Purpose in the Defence and Offence of both the United States of America, and Europe,” the island is “second to none.”

“Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defence will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived,” he wrote. ”It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!”

The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the U.S. military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defence and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO.

Trump said last month that the U.S. would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” including “building two very major military bases.”

By Stefanie Dazio and David Keyton

items.title: Judge extends order blocking Trump from banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from White House
items.description: A U.S. judge on Tuesday extended an order blocking U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, a pivotal operational development for the organizations as the extraordinary case — pitting the president against the media that cover him — makes its way through the legal system.

(AP Photo/John Minchillo)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">John Minchillo</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A U.S. judge on Tuesday extended an order blocking U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, a pivotal operational development for the organizations as the extraordinary case — pitting the president against the media that cover him — makes its way through the legal system.
items.body:
A U.S. judge has extended an order blocking U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, broadening his support for the journalists by arguing that the restriction violates their constitutional rights to free speech as well as due process.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in the extraordinary case pitting the president against the news outlets that cover him. In a victory for the journalists, Kelly expanded a previous, temporary ruling that the administration had violated the news outlets’ Fifth Amendment right to due process.

In a late-night ruling Tuesday, he also sided with a second argument by the outlets: that Trump’s ban breached their First Amendment right to free speech.

Kelly rejected Trump’s reasoning that the ban was driven by policy goals, such as protecting national security. He argued the ban was the result of Trump’s stated belief that the outlets’ reporting was inaccurate and biased.

“Simply put,” Kelly wrote, “That is unlawful viewpoint discrimination” -- the government taking action against types of speech or coverage it does not like.

“Still,” he added in his late-night order, “no one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”

But Trump’s standoff with the press is far from over. Kelly’s order did not address whether Trump can ban the three outlets from the rotating pool of broadcast networks that cover the president in tight spaces and share the reporting.

Stepped-up disputes between the president and the press

The fight reflects Trump’s increasing combativeness against news outlets and reporters whose content he does not like -- including sharply curtailing Pentagon access for the press corps that covers the Defense Department. Trump or other parts of the executive branch have also, in policy and in the courts, grappled with The Wall Street Journal, The Associated Press and The New York Times -- in addition to using the FCC to target broadcast networks.

The case of the three news outlets is increasingly messy and expensive. After the five-outlet rotating pool stood by CNN and canceled its coverage of Trump, the Justice Department over the weekend announced it was investigating whether those five companies violated antitrust laws in doing so.

Kelly’s ruling stood largely by the news outlets. He wrote that without a preliminary injunction blocking Trump’s ban, the outlets “are likely to suffer irreparable harm, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest tip in their favor.”

An email to the Justice Department, which is arguing the case on behalf of the administration, was not immediately returned. The White House also did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment.

Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the three media organizations, hailed the judge’s ruling.

“When the President issued his `ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment,” Boutrous said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this `unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future.”

Judge says no warning given before banishment

Kelly, who was nominated to the bench by Trump, previously ordered the White House to restore the reporters’ “hard pass” press credentials while he weighed their claims. With that temporary order expiring Tuesday, the judge issued a preliminary injunction that preserves the status quo indefinitely while the case is pending.

Kelly said that, “to put it mildly,” the White House didn’t give the plaintiffs any warning that they were in danger of losing their hard passes before Trump’s Sept. 18 social media post about their bans.

The judge also said the impact of the White House ban goes far beyond a single reporter’s ability to do their job.

“The ban threatens to cut off all Plaintiffs’ access to the White House press area--a space open to many of their competitors--thereby restricting their ability to observe happenings there firsthand, immediately report on those activities, and try to engage with government officials,” the judge wrote.

Hard passes give journalists who regularly cover the White House longer term access to its campus without having to get permission ahead of time.

The government asked Kelly to suspend his own decision pending an appeal, but the judge said it didn’t justify that request. Kelly said the bans impacted a total of 78 reporters at the three news organizations.

Earlier judicial action against White House had been only temporary

Trump provided no notice before announcing the bans in a Sept. 18 social media post, which criticized their reporting as “fake news.” Kelly temporarily blocked the bans on Sept. 24 at the request of the news outlets, which jointly filed a lawsuit in Washington, D.C.

Attorneys for the outlets have described Trump’s move as “unprecedented and blatantly unconstitutional” under the First and Fifth amendments. They argued that it’s illegal for Trump to punish the journalists because he doesn’t like the content of their reporting.

“The ban also inflicts an injury on all news media organizations -- which now risk a similar fate if they engage in fact-based, independent reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable,” plaintiffs’ lawyers wrote.

Government lawyers argued that access to the White House is a privilege -- not a right -- and said the president can impose the bans to protect national security and to stem the spread of misinformation.

“The White House is the official residence and workplace of the President,” Justice Department attorneys wrote. “Presidents have had a relationship with the press since the beginning. They have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially from administration to administration.”

Hallie Golden and Michael Kunzelman, The Associated Press

Associated Press reporter Rebecca Boone contributed.

items.title: Sudden Starlink limits sap Ukraine drone power as Kyiv fears U.S. intelligence squeeze
items.description: Ukrainian drones lost some of their fighting capacity after restrictions were suddenly imposed on the battlefield use of the country’s U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals, officials said Wednesday as the capital endured another night of missile attacks.

(AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Evgeniy Maloletka</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Ukrainian drones lost some of their fighting capacity after restrictions were suddenly imposed on the battlefield use of the country’s U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals, officials said Wednesday as the capital endured another night of missile attacks.
items.body:
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian drones lost some of their fighting capacity after restrictions were suddenly imposed on the battlefield use of the country’s U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals, officials said Wednesday as the capital endured another night of missile attacks.

At the same time, Ukraine did not receive the usual advance warning from its Western partners of the devastating Russian ballistic missiles that have struck Kyiv for two consecutive nights, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, triggering fears that Ukraine is being starved of vital intelligence, especially from the U.S.

Zelenskyy did not specify which partners he was talking about when referring to the lack of warning. U.S. President Donald Trump has said the U.S. has not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

The developments frustrated the Ukrainian military and deepened fears that Kyiv’s relationship with Washington is unraveling.

Ukrainian officials fear U.S. support for the war effort is falling away after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and isolate Putin.

Trump said Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end his country’s war with Russia and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.

Trump’s efforts to stop the fighting have resulted in no progress.

Starlink is an essential tool for Ukraine

Ukrainian officials are concerned that U.S. support, especially related to the sharing of military intelligence and the use of American tech titan Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications system, may be in jeopardy.

Musk’s SpaceX overnight imposed a speed limit on Ukraine’s Starlink terminals mounted on drones, Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, said on social media. The restriction disrupted operations, including making the slower-flying attack drones easier targets for Russian defences.

Starlink is a vital tool for the Ukrainian military, both in offensive and defensive operations. The network is used for long-range drone missions, interceptor air defence systems and front-line logistics, Beskrestnov said.

“Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” Beskrestnov said, without elaborating.

Neither SpaceX nor the White House offered any immediate comment.

Kyiv got no warning about initial ballistic missile attack, official says

Yurii Ihnat, Ukraine’s air force spokesman, said there was no warning of an initial Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday night, although Kyiv was warned about three later waves of missiles.

A lawmaker on Ukraine’s parliamentary Defence Committee told The Associated Press that intelligence sharing with international partners has not stopped. The lawmaker spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to give statements to the press.

Five people were killed and 36 injured in a Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital that lasted from Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning, Kyiv police said.

Russia keeps bombing Ukraine’s power grid despite Trump’s truce demand

Zelenskyy voiced outrage Wednesday over Russia’s continuing aerial bombardment of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump’s demand for a ceasefire.

“We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond -- and to respond forcefully” to Russia’s ongoing aerial barrages, Zelenskyy said in a social media post Wednesday.

“Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation,” he said.

Moscow’s forces pounded Ukraine’s power grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, for the third straight night, Zelenskyy said, after Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed not to strike energy infrastructure 4 1/2 years after Moscow’s forces invaded.

Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has agreed to halt Ukraine’s monthslong campaign targeting Russian oil refineries that caused fuel shortages for Russians. Ukraine’s last reported hit on an oil refinery was Friday.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that details of the energy ceasefire are still being decided. “The work in that direction is continuing,” he told reporters.

Russia hits three Kyiv power plants in attack, causing outages

The Russian Defence Ministry said in a statement Wednesday that its forces attacked Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in Kyiv, the wider Kyiv region and the northeastern Kharkiv region overnight, striking a total of six power plants.

Russian forces hit all three of Kyiv’s combined heat and power plants overnight into Wednesday, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. At least 600,000 people were left without power, Zelenskyy said.

Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and Kharkiv overnight, Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine claims it is pushing Russia back on the battlefield

Ukrainian officials say they are pushing back Russian forces in eastern Ukraine, which Russia’s bigger army has been trying to capture for years.

Ukraine has liberated 277 square kilometres (107 square miles) in the operation that started in the summer, Ukraine’s Third Army Corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said Wednesday.

It was not possible to independently verify the claim, and Russian officials did not comment.

Zelenskyy visits London for talks on more help in the war

Zelenskyy arrived Wednesday in London for talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham as Kyiv and its European supporters race to shore up Ukrainian defences. The Ukrainian leader could go to Brussels to attend a European Union summit later this week.

European leaders fear Moscow’s wider ambitions on the continent and accuse Russia of sabotage as part of a hybrid war on the continent. They seek to keep Washington on Ukraine’s side.

Burnham told the House of Commons that Ukraine is facing “a dark and difficult moment” and that Zelenskyy won’t go away “empty-handed.”

“What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back,” he said.

Analysts noted that Trump’s latest moves girded Europe into standing firm behind Kyiv.

“Ahead of a tough winter for Ukraine, Donald Trump’s swing back toward Russia bodes ill,” Rym Momtaz of the Carnegie Europe think tank wrote Tuesday. “But instead of panicking, Kyiv’s European allies are focusing on action.”

Ukraine attacks a Russian data centre with long-range drones

Ukraine is trying to fight back with attacks on other targets on Russian soil.

Russian air defences overnight downed 902 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions, illegally annexed Crimea and the waters of the Azov Sea, the Russian Defence Ministry said in a separate statement Wednesday.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 493 drones flew toward the capital region. Most were downed far away, and 180 were intercepted as they approached the Russian capital, he said. He did not report any damage or casualties.

In Russia’s Saratov region, one person was killed and several residential buildings were damaged, Gov. Roman Busargin said.

Russia’s state-backed Sberbank confirmed an attack on its Saratov data centre, once slated to become Europe’s biggest data centre.

Russian state news agency Tass quoted Alexander Vedyakhin, Sberbank’s first deputy chairman of the board, as saying that Sberbank systems were operating normally.

By Hanna Arhirova, Samya Kullab and Barry Hatton

Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal. Associated Press Writer Jill Lawless in London contributed.

items.title: China’s trade surplus nears record as pressure mounts from trading partners
items.description: China’s exports surged 36.3 per cent in September from a year earlier, its customs agency said, putting the country on track to surpass last year’s record.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Trucks loaded with container move through a container terminal port in Shanghai, China Monday, June 9, 2025. (Chinatopix Via AP)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: China’s exports surged 36.3 per cent in September from a year earlier, its customs agency said, putting the country on track to surpass last year’s record.
items.body:
HONG KONG — China’s exports surged 36.3 per cent in September from a year earlier, its customs agency said Wednesday, putting the country on track to surpass last year’s record trade surplus even as pressure mounts from trading partners, including the European Union, to rebalance trade.

The increase beat economists’ expectations and was stronger than the 25 per cent year-on-year growth in August. High-tech goods including semiconductors and automobiles helped fuel its rising shipments overseas.

September’s export growth pace was the fastest since February, according to a compilation of official data by FactSet.

Imports climbed 31 per cent in September year-on-year, also accelerating from August’s 28.2 per cent rise. Still, China recorded a US$133.5 billion trade surplus last month, widening from US$119.1 billion in August.

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

For the first nine months, China’s trade surplus reached US$938.1 billion, with expectations growing that it could surpass last year’s full-year US$1.2 trillion record.

Strong exports have helped drive China’s overall economic growth this year, at a time when domestic consumption and investment remained sluggish, weighed on by a yearslong real estate sector downturn.

However, China’s export resilience now faces mounting challenges, said Ecaterina Bigos, a senior market strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management.

“While U.S.-China trade tensions have eased somewhat, the EU’s push to rebalance directly targets high-value exports,” she said.

The U.S. has launched an ongoing probe against China and other trading partners this year on their excess industrial capacity, although Washington and Beijing last month reached an agreement to extend their trade truce and cut tariffs on US$60 billion worth of goods.

The 27-nation EU has particularly been struggling to rebalance a trade deficit exceeding US$1.1 billion a day with China. EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič, following his visit to Beijing where he met his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao last week, said a deal has been reached with Beijing, including halving Chinese hybrid car imports into the EU over the next few years.

Many of China’s trading partners are facing weak growth prospects and are fearful of their manufacturing industries being overrun by exports from China, said Eswar Prasad, a professor of economics and trade policy at Cornell University.

As talks about rebalancing trade with China grew, Chinese Premier Li Qiang said Wednesday at a landmark trade fair in the southern city of Guangzhou that the country is willing to import more high-quality goods, especially high-value-added products, and that it acts as both a “super seller” and a “super buyer,” according to an official readout of his speech.

Policymakers have also pointed to an undervalued yuan, China’s currency, against the U.S. dollar contributing to Chinese exports being cheaper overseas when compared with goods from other countries, adding to trade imbalances.

China’s central bank has said it has “no need or intent” to gain competitive advantages through currency devaluation and that its trade growth has been driven by its industrial competitiveness in the global market.

Between January and September, China’s semiconductor exports soared 108.1 per cent year-on-year in terms of value, customs data showed. Its exports of automatic data processing equipment and parts jumped 54.6 per cent, while auto exports rose 54.3 per cent, driven by an increased global demand for Chinese electric vehicles and hybrids.

China’s trade surplus and its high-tech export model depend on open markets, Bigos said, and while diversifying its exports into markets such as Southeast Asia and Latin America can help, it cannot fully substitute for Western demand.

  • Latest updates on international news here

The country’s reliance on high-tech exports, meanwhile, could face challenges as some U.S. technology industry leaders called for a global slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence for safety reasons.

“A slowdown in the global AI investment cycle could pose a greater threat to China’s export growth than trade restrictions imposed by other countries,” said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board.

Chinese leaders have set an annual economic growth target of 4.5 to five per cent for 2026.

This week, the International Monetary Fund lowered its forecast for China’s 2026 economic growth to 4.5 per cent, down 0.1 percentage point from its previous projection, as it warned that the country’s robust exports were unable to fully offset domestic weaknesses.

While Chinese officials have highlighted the need to bolster domestic demand, analysts believe that has yet to become a priority for this year even after authorities recently rolled out new measures to help lift its economy, including subsidies for homebuyers’ mortgage interest payments.

Chan Ho-him, The Associated Press

items.title: U.S. inflation worsened last month to 3.7% in sign that prices remain elevated as midterm elections near
items.description: U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes, and air fares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before the midterm elections that have focused heavily on issues related to affordability.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A woman pushes a shopping cart as she leaves a grocery store in Arlington Heights, Ill., Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Nam Y. Huh</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes, and air fares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before the midterm elections that have focused heavily on issues related to affordability.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gasoline and many other goods and services became more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before midterm elections that have focused heavily on affordability.

The consumer price index rose 3.7 per cent in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4 per cent in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6 per cent from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4 per cent increase the previous month.

The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn’t all linked to oil and gas, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6 per cent in September from a year ago, up from 2.4 per cent the previous month and higher than economists had expected. And they climbed 0.3 per cent from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed’s 2 per cent target.

Higher inflation will likely put more pressure on the Fed to lift its key interest rate at its next meeting Oct. 27-28. Economists noted that the report showed price increases were spread more broadly across the economy than in recent months.

“The report was worse than expected,” Bill Adams, chief U.S. economist at Fifth Third Bank, said in a note to clients. “Price increases were widespread .... Consumer demand seems to be holding up better than the downbeat consumer surveys would suggest, helping businesses maintain pricing power.”

Wednesday’s figures are the last major inflation data to be released before the upcoming elections. Ongoing inflation has taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17 per cent of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living issue. And only 26 per cent approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.

Gas prices jumped 9.1 per cent just from August to September, the government’s consumer price index report said. Rising gas costs are a highly visible sign of inflation and often drive down measures of consumer sentiment about the economy.

With fuel much more expensive, air fares rose 1.2 per cent last month and have soared 22 per cent compared with a year ago. Hotel prices rose 2 per cent from August to September and are up 4.4 per cent compared with a year earlier.

Consumers saw some relief in grocery prices, which actually declined 0.1 per cent last month and are up just 1.8 per cent from a year ago. Ground beef prices fell 0.8 per cent in September, though they are still up 5.4 per cent from last year.

The cost of toys, new and used cars, sporting goods, and shoes all rose at a rapid clip last month, the government said.

The government also said Wednesday that Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6 per cent cost of living increase, based on the inflation figures.

The Middle East and Russia-Ukraine conflicts have also sharply inflated the cost of diesel fuel, which is used by long-haul trucks and will likely inflate shipping expense, which in turn could push up prices for a range of goods.

Ralph Newhouse, CEO of Chefman, which makes countertop appliances, said that rising diesel prices could force him to raise prices in the coming months.

The Mahwah, N.J.-based company, which makes milk frothers, air fryers, blenders and other appliances in China, last increased its prices in 2024. This year, it has used its US$20 million in tariff refunds to offset the rise in fuel costs, but may not be able to do so much longer.

“We’re at the point right now that if we continue to see any additional rises in (diesel) prices, then these conversations are going to be forced upon us. We just day by day, hope and pray that we don’t have to have this conversation.”

Fed rate path

U.S. Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn’t moving quickly enough back to the central bank’s target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9 per cent.

Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year.

Still, Wednesday’s report has led many Wall Street investors to project that the Fed will now act in two weeks. The odds of a rate increase at the central bank’s October meeting have doubled, though remain at just 50-50, according to futures pricing tracked by CME Fedwatch.

Stock prices fell slightly after the report, while greater expectations for rate hikes pushed up bond yields, which will raise borrowing costs throughout the economy.

By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war’s disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can’t address those bottlenecks.

Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It’s already pushed up the price of air fares about 22 per cent from a year ago.

Prices at the pump have ticked lower in the past two weeks to a nationwide average of US$4.33 a gallon, according to AAA, though they remain higher than a month ago.

Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients.

  • Latest updates on international news here

The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones.

Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge.

On September 1, Nintendo increased the price for its Switch 2 gaming system by 11 per cent to US$499.99. And Apple’s newest iPhone, the iPhone 17, cost about 10 per cent more than its previous upgrade, though some of that likely reflects greater capabilities.

Christopher Rugaber, The Associated Press

items.body:
MONTREAL — Montreal-area home sales were down 11.6 per cent year-over-year in September as the province’s real estate board says residential markets across Quebec are “a long way” from reaching a balance between inventory and demand.

The Quebec Professional Association of Real Estate Brokers says 3,082 residential properties changed hands throughout the month in the Montreal census metropolitan area, down from 3,486 in September 2025.

Hélène Bégin, the board’s senior economist, says that although competition has eased since last year in the single-family home market, sellers “remain in a strong negotiating position” across every area of the province.

In the Montreal area, there were 7,494 new listings in September, up 7.2 per cent year-over-year, while total inventory rose 19.9 per cent to 21,793 units for sale.

Home prices were slightly higher year-over-year, led by a 2.5 per cent increase in the median price of a plex to $861,000.

The median price of a single-family home rose 0.5 per cent year-over-year to $635,000 in September, while the median price of a condominium was flat at $430,000.

OTTAWA — Statistics Canada says the total value of building permits issued in Canada in August rose $1.1 billion month-over-month to $13.6 billion, boosted by strength in the residential sector.

The agency says construction intentions for the homebuilding sector rose $1.1 billion to $8.5 billion in August.

The increase came as permits for multi-unit buildings rose to $5.8 billion, while the total value of permits for single-family homes edged down to $2.6 billion.

The value of non-residential building permits edged lower by $29.8 million to $5.1 billion in August.

The move came as plans for commercial construction fell $380 million to $2.2 billion, offset in part by a $317.3-million gain in the industrial sector which totalled $1.1 billion.

The institutional building component rose $32.9 million to $1.8 billion.

items.title: Demographic changes to shrink Canada's workforce: Bank of Canada
items.description: ‘Businesses need to understand it to develop new markets and products, invest in productivity-enhancing technology and help their workers gain skills for the future’
items.content: <p>‘Businesses need to understand it to develop new markets and products, invest in productivity-enhancing technology and help their workers gain skills for the future’</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/036/0363_639274915805105444.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: ‘Businesses need to understand it to develop new markets and products, invest in productivity-enhancing technology and help their workers gain skills for the future’
items.body:
Demographic changes will shrink the Canadian workforce and could push up wages in some sectors, according to an explainer from the Bank of Canada, which said an aging population and lower immigration are reducing the number of people working.

Canada's population grew by only 0.5% in 2025 – the weakest pace in more than a century, according to the bank. For most of the past 50 years, annual growth held at about 1.2%.

Why is Canada's labour supply tightening?

Canada's birth rate has been below replacement level for more than five decades, the Bank said, and immigration – which long filled that gap – has been falling since Ottawa began cutting levels in 2024.

Statistics Canada's quarterly estimates, released Sept. 23, 2026, show the population rose by 189,425 people, or about 0.5%, between July 1, 2025, and July 1, 2026, to 41,798,407. The population fell by 7,225 between Oct. 1, 2025, and Jan. 1, 2026. Alberta accounted for about 40% of the national increase over the year, while Ontario grew by less than 0.3%.

Under the 2026–2028 Immigration Levels Plan from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), the target for new temporary worker arrivals is 230,000 in 2026, including 60,000 under the Temporary Foreign Worker (TFW) Program. Ottawa aims to cut the temporary population to less than 5% of the total by the end of 2027, while holding permanent resident admissions at 380,000 a year and transitioning up to 33,000 temporary workers to permanent residency in 2026 and 2027.

The Bank noted that temporary workers often fill jobs in sectors with labour shortages, such as restaurants and agriculture, while highly skilled immigrants bring scarce expertise in fields such as computer engineering.

For employers that relied on these workers, the effects are visible. Some Prince Edward Island businesses are cutting staff hours and extending shifts as federal immigration cuts shrink the labour pool, while those still hiring them face heightened immigration law compliance scrutiny and audits.

Aging workforce raises retention and succession stakes

Canada's median age was about 26 in 1971 and is now above 40, according to Statistics Canada data cited by the Bank. Most baby boomers have reached retirement age, and fewer young people are entering the labour market to replace them.

The Bank said labour shortages could raise wages in some sectors, potentially feeding into inflation. Older Canadians also spend more on health care, adding demand in that sector.

For HR leaders, that means sharper competition for talent in sectors such as health care, alongside the loss of institutional knowledge as long-tenured staff retire. Succession planning becomes more pressing, though employers should tread carefully when asking older workers about their retirement plans, given the risk of age discrimination claims.

In the same speech, Macklem pointed to the role of employers as the economy adjusts to structural change. "Businesses need to understand it to develop new markets and products, invest in productivity-enhancing technology and help their workers gain skills for the future," he said.

items.title: Vancouver opens the door to convertible balconies
items.description: Developers say retractable glass systems can make balconies more usable during the city’s rainy months
items._ogDesc: Developers say retractable glass systems can make balconies more usable during the city’s rainy months
items.body:
Having a balcony is nice for people who want to enjoy some fresh air without leaving home. But what about balconies that could be closed off to shield residents from Vancouver’s rain and wind, and reduce the noise from the streets below?

A number of companies and developers are introducing the concept to the region—convertible balconies that can be temporarily enclosed or opened, usually using retractable glass panels.

Vancouver city council recently updated its design guidelines to recognize fully retractable glass balcony systems. The changes will take effect Oct. 27, according to the city.

“Balconies with glass panels that slide, fold, or stack open can still be considered outdoor space, as long as the glass can be fully opened, the balcony is not permanently heated, and it continues to function primarily as a balcony rather than an indoor room,” the City of Vancouver said in a statement.

The City also approved removing restrictions on how much balcony space can be excluded from a building’s floor area calculations, effective Oct. 27, giving developers more flexibility to include larger balconies in new apartment buildings.

“These changes make it easier to build larger balconies and clarify that retractable glass weather screens can be used without the balcony being treated as enclosed indoor space, provided the guidelines are met,” the city said.

Some B.C. developers and companies are applauding the changes, saying convertible balconies give residents more flexibility in how they use their living space and could make balconies more usable.

“[It’s a] big deal … that Vancouver has recognized, like many other municipalities,” said Michael Geller, a Vancouver-based developer, real estate consultant and retired architect. He is working with Finnish firm Lumon Group to introduce retractable glass panels for balconies to B.C. and has been advocating for the concept for years.

Other municipalities, including Burnaby, North Vancouver, Langley, West Vancouver and Victoria, have already allowed the technology, according to Geller.

“Sometimes it's nice to have the window open and get the fresh air, and sometimes it's nice to close because it's a bit cold [or it's raining], and it's also quite noisy driving along,” he said.

“It really makes the balcony much more usable.”

Vancouver-based Concord Pacific Developments Inc. is building a three-building high-rise complex in the Metrotown area that’s scheduled for completion next year. One of the selling points for the project is its large convertible balconies, according to Terry Hui, president and CEO of Concord.

An 807-square-foot two-bedroom unit at Concord Metrotown, which costs more than $1.2 million, has more than 500 square feet of outdoor space with retractable glass panels that Hui said would significantly increase residents’ living space.

“The market really likes it,” said Hui, noting that about 85 per cent of the roughly 1,400 units have been presold.

“Families are very excited about it as well, to be able to have the kids on the outside space while the parents try to maintain their sanity inside. …We have one buyer that's excited about having his office outside because he likes fresh air.”

Not appealing to cost-sensitive buyers

The convertible balcony offers residents more flexibility, but it remains a premium feature given the costs and housing affordability challenges in Metro Vancouver, according to industry insiders.

“I think it's a great idea and it's a great use of space,” said Michael Stewart, a Vancouver-based real estate agent and blogger. “It makes the balcony useful for more days of the year.”

He said he sees the product appealing to buyers who value large balconies and are willing to pay a premium for the units, but less attractive to average buyers because of the additional cost it adds to already-expensive homes in Metro Vancouver.

“It's a premium thing because the people who are price-sensitive are primarily not buying the bigger, higher-end, nicer units with the large balconies,” said Stewart.

“For smaller balconies, it doesn't really make sense to [install the system].”

Stewart said he could see the product becoming more popular in markets where activity is stronger and prices are rising, as buyers may be more willing to pay for upgrades. That, however, is not the case in Metro Vancouver right now.

Geller said cost is one of the main challenges to wider adoption of convertible balcony systems in the region. He did not disclose the specific price of installing Lumon’s retractable glass system but said it can range from several thousand dollars to more than $10,000.

“But the cost will come down as it becomes more common,” he said.

Given the current tax and regulatory framework for property development, it can be difficult for developers to make a profit selling small, inexpensive units because of the costs involved, so many choose to offer more features to target high-end buyers, according to Stewart.

The convertible balcony feature, as well as other features such as EV chargers, could help projects stand out in a softer market and give them a competitive advantage, he added.

“The market dynamic is for the developers to offer more to win market share in a smaller market,” said Stewart.

“If [buyers] have a choice between a big balcony that isn't convertible and a big balcony that is convertible, and maybe the price difference isn't much, they probably would choose the convertible balcony.”

Geller believes the City of Vancouver’s approval will help make convertible balconies a standard feature in new housing projects over time.

“I would suggest that just like air conditioning is becoming almost standard in many good quality high-rise buildings, 10 years from now, most new apartments will have it in Vancouver because it makes a lot of sense,” he said.

items.title: Millions of pink salmon are returning to spawn on Canada’s West Coast. But why?
items.description: Millions more of a species of salmon are returning to spawn up the Fraser River on Canada’s West Coast, but exactly why remains hotly disputed and solving that puzzle could have major implications for wild salmon stocks and coastal communities.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Atlantic salmon swim in the open net pens at a MOWI Canada West fish farm near Port Hardy, B.C. The image was supplied by MOWI Canada West.]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Millions more of a species of salmon are returning to spawn up the Fraser River on Canada’s West Coast, but exactly why remains hotly disputed and solving that puzzle could have major implications for wild salmon stocks and coastal communities.
items.body:
PORT HARDY, B.C. -- Millions more of a species of salmon are returning to spawn up the Fraser River on Canada’s West Coast, but exactly why remains hotly disputed, and the answer could have major implications for wild salmon stocks and coastal communities.

Some First Nations, in concert with environmental groups, have attributed this surge to the shutdown of dozens of salmon farms and are urging the federal government to enact a promised ban of the remainder of those farms by 2029.

But a W5 investigation has revealed a confidential internal assessment where federal government scientists say salmon farming operations pose a “minimal risk” to wild stocks and recommended reopening some of them, as the government itself is not outwardly committing to that ban.

“Farm presence (or absence) is only one of many variables, and current evidence does not demonstrate a causal link,” the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) said in a statement to W5, as another scientist suggested that surging salmon species, the pink salmon, may simply be doing better than other species in warming oceans.

A lot hinges on getting the science right: coastal communities are bracing for the impact of more salmon farm closures that could shed hundreds more jobs in what was once a billion-dollar industry, affect a valued way of life for First Nations, and change what Canadian consumers put on their plates.

The Discovery Islands: a pink salmon surge

Aboard his motorboat in the waters off the Discovery Islands, about 200 km northwest of Vancouver between Vancouver Island and the B.C. mainland, researcher Jody Erickson says he has noticed something incredible.

A seine net dropped from his motorboat can catch hundreds of young salmon smolts at a time, and Erickson draws up a few of them in a clear plastic case to see several different species: pink, chum and Chinook.

“What I would call very happy and healthy-looking fish right now,” he said. “No lice.”

It’s a far cry from what Erickson says he used to see in these waters a decade ago: juvenile salmon laden with parasites sticking to their skin, Erickson said. He still carries with him samples from those days that show small fish pockmarked with the parasites.

“They’re dying near fish farms. That’s what I see,” he said.

The Discovery Islands are a crucial thoroughfare for young salmon, who breed far up the freshwater rivers on B.C.’s coast, including the Fraser River, and then swim through these waters, around Vancouver Island, before making it out to sea.

Those islands, and the salmon farms that used to be there, were singled out by the Cohen Commission, a judicial inquiry that was called in 2009 after a salmon stock collapse.

Cohen pointed to many stressors that could affect the health of B.C. salmon, including warming waters, and recommended closing salmon farms in the Discovery Islands unless the federal fisheries minister is satisfied those farms pose at most a minimal risk to migrating sockeye salmon.

In 2019, the federal government followed through, refusing dozens of licences around the Discovery Islands, and then from the nearby Broughton Archipelago as a precaution. About half of all B.C. salmon farms are now gone.

A study by the Salmon Coast Field Station concluded that numbers of one species of lice dropped in the area once the salmon farms were removed, which could mean more salmon survive the long journey out to sea, said Research Crew Lead Kate Medcalf.

“As they out-migrate in these small sizes, they’re incredibly, incredibly vulnerable to parasitism and other stressors in the environment,” Medcalf said.

Erickson believes he is seeing the results of having fewer lice in the strait now.

“It’s very hopeful, because it shows that if we remove the fish farms, the fish can come back, really, really remarkably fast, faster than even I would have thought,” Erickson said.

Shuttered farms: the human cost

Nearby where Erickson cast his nets are what remains of several salmon farming operations. Some of them have been converted to other uses, while some have left no trace.

Those shutdowns meant lost jobs, and a narrowed future for the workers who hoped to launch long-term careers, said Kaitlin Guitard, a lab manager for one farm company, Mowi Canada West.

In an interview on the dock of one of the remaining farms, in the Queen Charlotte Strait near Port Hardy, she said she has lost hundreds of co-workers.

“It’s awful, it really is,” Guitard said. “I was relocated. But I think the hardest part for me was a lot of people that I worked with had either been laid off or could not wait around for certainty and had left.”

Guitard is among those fighting for the future of these farms, saying Canada needs the jobs and the food those farms produced.

Mowi Canada West’s production dropped from 40,000 tonnes a year, before the farms started to be removed in 2019, to 20,000 tonnes a year.

“The impact has been fairly devastating to the industry. We’ve lost 45 per cent of our production,” said Brian Kingzett, of the B.C. Salmon Farmers Association.

Kingzett says he’s aware that some farms have lice outbreaks, and that they do their best to manage them. But he doesn’t buy the connection drawn by researchers between his farms and the salmon collapse.

“We’ve had nine significant studies that have all identified that we can coexist with wild salmon, and we are continuing to innovate to further reduce any potential risks,” he said.

Rising numbers for salmon species; others are falling

Kingzett points to tracking by the Pacific Salmon Commission, a regulatory body run jointly by the Canadian and United States governments.

They use underwater sound waves and sonar to estimate the number of salmon passing the Mission hydroacoustic station in Mission, B.C., as they head up the Fraser River.

According to the commission figures, the number of pink salmon, which has a two-year life cycle, has doubled since 2019, from about 8.5 million to 17.7 million in 2025.

But the picture for another species of salmon, which has a four-year life cycle, is much less clear.

Promising returns of 8.1 million sockeye passing its station in 2025 were followed by disappointing returns under 3 million in 2026.

That figure was lower than 2022, when the Discovery Islands farms had been removed, and lower than in 2018 and 2014, when all the salmon farms were operating.

The DFO also monitors salmon escapement numbers by region along the coast. In region 13, which includes the Discovery Islands, coho and pink salmon are increasing, but chinook and sockeye salmon are not.

The connection between salmon farms and the health of wild stocks was also doubted by the DFO, which advised the fisheries minister in 2023 that its preferred option was to re-licence all 15 salmon farms in the Discovery Islands.

“Current Departmental science advice includes nine risk assessments that were completed specifically to advise the Department on the issue of licencing in the Discovery Islands, found that pathogen transmission from Atlantic salmon farms in the Discovery Islands poses minimal risk to Fraser River sockeye salmon population abundance and diversity under existing fish health management practices,” the department wrote.

The licenses were not re-issued. In 2024, the federal government proposed a draft transition plan that would ban open net pen salmon farming by 2029.

However, there has been no final transition plan released since.

In response to questions from CTV News about whether the federal government plans to follow through with the 2029 ban, a statement from Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson didn’t mention it.

“Pacific salmon are iconic to the West Coast and protecting and rebuilding wild salmon populations is a priority for our government,” the statement said, pointing to investments the government has made in three new salmon hatcheries, and consultation with stakeholders in B.C. this summer.

“There is no single solution to the challenges facing wild Pacific salmon, which is why we are taking a comprehensive approach to protecting and rebuilding these stocks,” she said.

Another school of thought

In his home in Nanaimo, B.C., retired fish scientist and winner of the Order of Canada Dick Beamish is convinced the answer to the mystery of the salmon returns lies farther out in the Pacific Ocean.

He points to studies that show pink salmon are surging not just in B.C. but worldwide, because they are better able to handle warming ocean temperatures.

“There will be populations in the north Pacific that are adapting to the ocean warming conditions better than others,” Beamish said in an interview.

Some species are coming back from their time in the ocean much smaller, on average, than in previous years, he said.

“What is probably happening with the warming that we’re seeing in the ocean is that there’s less food being produced that’s allowing salmon to accumulate the energy that they need to survive ocean winters,” Beamish said.

“That’s just a hypothesis. What we really need is scientific studies that are going to take a look at how this ocean warming is changing the overall food availability for salmon once they get into the open ocean,” he said.

Raising salmon on land?

Environmental groups are convinced that salmon farms are a threat and are pushing for alternatives to raise salmon on land.

In Port McNeill, in a cavernous warehouse only about a kilometre from where the Nimpkish River flows into the Queen Charlotte Strait, there are fish who will never see the ocean at all.

They’re grown in large circular tanks in a facility called Kuterra, built by the Namgis First Nation in 2013 for $10 million as a demonstration project to prove that a land-based aquaculture industry is possible in B.C.

More than 10 years in, the project is still going, with some changes. The facility used to produce salmon but has found it’s easier to produce trout, said Chief Don Svanvik of the Namgis First Nation.

“It’s incredible. It’s a big investment,” Svanvik said in an interview in Port McNeill. “But it’s happening. If it was easy, everybody would be doing it.”

A study commissioned by the B.C. government in 2021 found that the experience of Kuterra may be hard to replicate, warning of high capital costs, difficulty obtaining power, and regulatory uncertainty.

“The results are not promising,” said the report, by Counterpoint Consulting, saying the estimated rate of return is too low at 8.7 per cent for a large farm and 5.8 per cent for a medium-sized farm.

“Those rates of return are far too low to attract the investment required to incentivize the development of a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) salmon farming industry in British Columbia,” the report said.

“We have concluded from our research and analysis that RAS development in BC is possible, but at smaller scales and not in isolation from the larger aquaculture sector currently operating in BC,” the report said.

Tony Allard, a businessman who is the chair of the environmental group Wild First, admits land-based farms can be “capital-intensive.”

But he said there are other advantages, pointing to another land-based farm near Tokyo, which he said saves on transportation costs because it’s right next to its market.

Allard said that there is investor interest in making these work, especially if the open net pen farming is shut down.

“It has proved the concept. It’s grown fish, and it’s sold them at a premium,” he said in an interview.

“And that’s where the growth of this industry is. So, keep the ban, no half-measures, and let’s grow this industry safely, sustainably, on land,” he said.

Imports filling the gaps

Canadian consumers may not be waiting around as foreign fish farms have rushed in to fill the gaps left by shuttered West Coast fish farms.

One major grocery chain, Loblaws, told CTV News in a statement that it sources salmon from a variety of Canadian and international suppliers, and prices vary based on a number of factors.

“Reduced domestic supply in recent years has meant we are relying more on imported salmon; however, Canadian salmon remains an important part of our assortment, and we will continue to source domestically where supply and market conditions allow,” the statement said.

In 2016, Canada imported about $90.5 million in fish categories including Atlantic salmon, according to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada and Statistics Canada. That number quadrupled to $356 million in 2025.

It was a similar surge from Norway, whose exports to Canada rose from $34 million to $158 million.

And Iceland’s exports surged 22 times, from $0.8 million to $20 million in the same time period.

“I think that’s a challenge for Canadians to wake up and turn around and look and say, is this something that we want? Do we want to import fish?” asked Richard Opala, a regulatory affairs manager at Mowi Canada West.

“Well, we can grow it here. Do we want to support jobs in other countries when we don’t have them here?” he said.

But critics of the fish farm industry say that Canadian wild stocks could be better protected if Canadians order from farms in ecosystems without competing salmon.

“The stakes are higher here than they are in Norway, where there are no longer any commercial fisheries,” said Kristi Miller, a scientist who used to work with the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans.

“It’s different here in British Columbia, because we still have large, abundant populations of wild fish. We still have commercial fisheries. We still have recreational fisheries, we still have Indigenous fisheries,” she said.

Coastal community worries

Some First Nations groups are concerned enough about the potential impact of salmon farms they are calling for the eviction of remaining salmon farms near Port Hardy.

“What wild salmon mean to First Nations all across the province is beyond valuation. It contributes to food security across the province. It is the basis of our culture and traditions. And is not an item we wish to see impacted while others make profits,” said Bob Chamberlin, chair of the First Nations Wild Salmon Alliance, at a news conference this month on Parliament Hill.

In Port Hardy, on northern Vancouver Island, Mayor Patricia Corbett-Labatt is concerned about what losing the remaining salmon farms would mean for her community.

“We are a fishing, logging, mining community. We’re resource based,” she said in an interview.

She said she is concerned about what would happen to the jobs, and by extension the community, if more farms are shut down.

“It would be very similar to when the mine closed here and there was a huge depression,” she said.

Over in the Queen Charlotte Strait, Guitard from Mowi takes a scoop of pellets and tosses it into an open pen. The fish respond by jumping.

She said she’s worried about what may be in store in 2029, when the ban is set to take effect, but is hopeful she can stay in her home in Campbell River.

“It’s awful, honestly. I’ve been here for six years. I have established a whole community, I have friends, it’s a lifestyle that I would love to live, but it really does rely solely on this industry continuing here.”

items.title: Affordability remains a drag – but CEO says Canadians still aspire to own a home
items.description: Despite a challenging housing market outlook RE/MAX Canada’s Kottick says Canadians still want to move, and are willing to compromise to do so
items.content: <p>Despite a challenging housing market outlook RE/MAX Canada’s Kottick says Canadians still want to move, and are willing to compromise to do so</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639275023114611598.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Despite a challenging housing market outlook RE/MAX Canada’s Kottick says Canadians still want to move, and are willing to compromise to do so
items.body:
Tariffs, economic uncertainty and affordability challenges may be hurting the national housing market – but Canadians are still clinging to the dream of homeownership despite those hurdles, according to RE/MAX Canada’s president.

The real estate giant’s latest housing market outlook, released last week, showed 65% of hopeful buyers surveyed are prepared to compromise in their efforts to own a home, including through relocation and cutting back on discretionary spending.

And Don Kottick, who’s helmed the organization as president since last year, told Canadian Mortgage Professional that the poll suggests homeownership appetite is still strong even with a sluggish market and challenging economic environment.

“Homeownership is still near and dear to the hearts of pretty much most Canadians,” he said. “Regardless of market conditions, regardless of headwinds, homeownership is still tied to who we are as Canadians.”

Widespread return to the city unlikely, says Kottick

Home affordability has improved modestly across many markets this year, although rising interest rates are eroding some of those gains. Some executives say the only solution to unlock a healthier market is for prices to drop even further.

But Kottick sees potential buyers who are on the verge of being able to afford a home taking pragmatic steps to get a purchase over the line.

“People are willing to sit a little longer in traffic to get that home that really appeals to their wants and their needs,” he said. “If they can get that bigger home [for less], they get better quality of life.”

The COVID-19 pandemic and the onset of a remote-working revolution pushed scores of buyers out of cramped apartments in big cities and toward more rural, spacious housing.

A hot topic of debate in the real estate sector since then is whether a ramping-up of return-to-office efforts could see buyers turn their attention back to cities and away from suburban and rural areas, but Kottick isn’t convinced.

“It’s not happening like, flip a switch and everybody’s back. It’s something that’s kind of a work in progress,” he said. “There’s a lot of discussion on it, a lot of talk on it – and probably a lot of resistance to it.”

Regional picture varies, but much will depend on BoC for 2027

About 32% of housing markets analyzed by RE/MAX’s latest report now sit in buyer’s market territory, a jump from 15.2% last year, as softer conditions emerge in many parts of the country.

Home sales were down in 81% of markets analyzed, the survey said. But while the outlook for the national market is cloudy, it’s often highlighted that the regional picture can vary widely from one province or city to the next – and prices actually increased in 56% of markets.

Some regional markets are still showing notable strength, Kottick said, with Northern Ontario cities including Sudbury, Thunder Bay, Kenora and Sault Ste. Marie seeing sellers’ market conditions holding.

Saskatoon and St. John’s, Newfoundland, meanwhile, are also bucking the broader national trend. “We still have these pockets that are really resilient, really strong,” Kottick said. “The recovery is definitely slower in some of the major markets where there’s been more price appreciation over time.”

Still, it goes without saying that the continuing trade war with the US and inflation fears as a result of the US-Iran war are keeping a lid on homebuying demand.

Rising oil prices have sent inflation expectations soaring in recent weeks, with chances of at least one Bank of Canada rate hike in the coming months also reportedly growing.

The central bank is scheduled to make its next decision at the end of this month, although at least one top economist has questioned the need for rate hikes – especially with the economy continuing to weaken.  

Kottick said the trajectory into next year will depend on those factors, and whether there’s good news ahead on the economic front.

“If we can get the macro headwinds resolved, we very well could see the market really pick up in 2027,” he said.

items.content: <p>Mortgage brokers will gather at Rebel Toronto on November 25 for the program’s 20th-anniversary gala</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639275163379725593.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Mortgage brokers will gather at Rebel Toronto on November 25 for the program’s 20th-anniversary gala
items.body:
Canada’s mortgage brokers will gather at Rebel Toronto on Wednesday, November 25, for the 20th Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs), the national recognition program presented by Canadian Mortgage Professional (CMP).

The shortlist is already set. In September, CMP named its 2026 excellence awardees, the final shortlisted candidates across 23 competitive categories. That makes the gala the night the results go public, and much of the broker channel’s networking happens there too. 

The business case for mortgage brokers

1. A milestone edition two decades in the making

The 2026 gala marks 20 years of the program recognizing the professionals, firms and leaders moving the Canadian mortgage industry forward. An event that has lasted two decades has outlived several rate cycles. That longevity is the reason a CMA carries weight with clients and lenders. 

2. The shortlist resolves live

Readers can already review the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards excellence awardees. Among them in Eastern Canada are Anthony Di Feo of Multi-Prêts Mortgages, Nicole Farrugia of Vine Group and Paul Meredith of PMT Mortgage Corp.

Winners in all 26 categories will be revealed at the gala, so attendees see the results first. 

3. The results are independently judged

The outcome is not decided by popularity. Winners are chosen through a points system that tallies the judging panel’s votes, and the excellence awardee with the highest score in each category takes the award.

CMP has profiled the five independent judges scoring this year’s submissions. Their backgrounds span academic research, regulatory law, federal housing policy and executive leadership in Canadian mortgage and finance.

The panel includes Andrey Pavlov, professor of finance at Simon Fraser University’s Beedie School of Business in Vancouver. 

4. A benchmark for your own 2027 plan

The judging criteria double as a business review. For broker categories, judges weigh loan volumes, year-over-year growth, lead generation, client retention, conversion rates and overall customer service.

Broker of the Year is awarded in three regions: Maritimes/Atlantic Canada, Eastern Canada and Western Canada. Only category winners advance to compete for the overall Canadian Broker of the Year title. 

5. Your lender partners in one room

The program recognizes business development managers (BDMs) and underwriters, not just brokers.

In the BDM categories, nominations coming directly from the broking community carry considerable weight.

The 2026 sponsors include CMI Canadian Mortgages Inc., Equitable Bank, Haventree Bank, MCAN Mortgage Corporation, RFA Mortgage Corporation and Real Property Solutions Inc.

With renewal volumes still elevated, a face-to-face conversation with a lender’s leadership team can be worth more than a dozen emails. 

6. The industry’s decision-makers, all in one place

The gala draws hundreds of leading mortgage professionals and senior executives from top organizations. Few other evenings put brokerage principals, network heads and lender executives in the same room. 

7. A preview of where the broker’s role is heading

Two categories are new this year: Mortgage Tech Innovator of the Year and The REMIC Award for Finfluencer of the Year.

The finfluencer category judges entrants partly on compliance awareness and adherence to Canadian regulatory and advertising guidelines for mortgage promotions. That is a signal of how digital advice is expected to mature. 

What to expect on the night

8. Recognition for the whole team

Brokerage and team categories are split at 25 employees, so smaller shops compete with peers of a similar size.

The evening also includes the Haventree Bank Award for Lifetime Achievement, the program’s highest honour, which has no finalists and is announced only at the ceremony. 

9. Recognition that pays off after the gala

Past winners say the award works long after the trophy is handed out. “Developers and investors need confidence in their advisor from day one,” said Akshay Gupta, a commercial real estate mortgage agent at Foundry Mortgage Capital Corp. in Toronto and the 2025 Young Achiever of the Year.

Kyle Benzies of DLC AIMI Collective Mortgage Group put it more directly: “Being a part of this, it’ll actually change the trajectory of my business.”

10. A well-run evening

The cocktail reception will run from 6 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. It will be followed by the awards ceremony and seated dinner until 10:30 p.m., then a post-awards celebration. The host is broadcaster Sonia Mangat, who appears on eTalk and CP24 Breakfast.

Entertainment will come from the five-piece band Soulfire and a Frank Sinatra tribute by Jesse Posa. 

Registration is open at canadianmortgageawards.com/register-now.

The post Canada’s Housing Crash Rivals US In 2008, But The Pain Is Hidden: BMO appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canada’s home prices fell more than 20%, but BMO says population growth may have masked the economic pain of the housing crash.
items.body:
Canada’s housing crash is close to rivalling the early 2000s crash in the US. In contrast, Canada seems relatively unscathed, despite being a smaller economy that’s more dependent on housing. BMO’s chief economist notes the country is better positioned to avoid a financial crisis, but its pain avoidance is partly an illusion—hidden by Canada’s aggressive use of immigration.

Canadian Home Prices Are Following The US Housing Crash

Source: BMO Capital Markets; CREA.

The Canadian housing correction is following the same trajectory as the U.S., but with a different outcome. Home prices in Canada have dropped 20.5% from the early-2022 peak, compared with 26% during the U.S. bust. However, Canada avoided a comparable economic collapse—its real GDP grew at an annualized pace of 1.7% over the four years since prices started falling. That’s only slightly below the 2.0% average for this century, which is remarkable considering the country’s housing-dependent economy.

“This is arguably the most significant home price correction ever for Canada, and yet the economy has managed to avoid serious collateral damage from the deep decline,” explains BMO Chief Economist Douglas Porter.

He notes Canada has seen only one “traditional” recession in the past 35 years. That was the Global Financial Crisis, with 2020 being a very different policy-induced shutdown. He clarifies, “… it’s not as if recessions never happen, they are now just extremely rare events, and it takes a near cataclysm to cause a full-scale downturn.”

How? There’s some clear factors that helped mitigate the worst of the fallout—at least on the surface.

Stronger Borrowers And Rate Cuts Helped Contain The Fallout

The bank sees the brief period of peak home prices as one of the key differentiators. Porter notes prices surged 50% over the final two years, containing the damage to a relatively small pool. The correction is also largely contained in two provinces, leaving prices relatively unscathed for almost half the country. A substantial wealth cushion also helps limit spending cutbacks, while an aging population increasingly supports consumption through non-employment income such as pensions. In fact, seniors (aged 65+) represented over 1 in 5 (22.4%) dollars of consumption in 2025.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

The bank also notes that the finances were stronger. Mortgage qualification hurdles, like the stress test, helped minimize the volume of overextended borrowers. Rate cuts began less than a year after rates peaked, softening the normalization shock. Overall, the headline data reveals an economy that’s darn near invincible.

Skeptical that a housing-based economy could survive a US-style housing correction with so little damage? There’s a good reason—the apparent escape may have been partly an illusion, according to Porter.

Canada Avoided A Financial Crisis, But It Didn’t Avoid The Pain

Porter believes Canada avoided the financial crisis, but avoiding the pain is partly an “illusion.” The population grew at an annualized pace of 2.8% over two years to early 2024, generally faster than GDP averaged. This helped to offset—possibly more than offset—any pullback in GDP. The economy grew, but the population grew faster—meaning less economic output per person, despite headline gains.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

Measured per person, real GDP per capita fell in four of five quarters during the 2022-23 stretch, falling more than 2% peak-to-trough. Unemployment also climbed more than 2 percentage points over that period, a rare combination. Porter says this has only occurred a handful of times in the past 60 years—and only during official recessions.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

“In other words, some of Canada’s Housing Houdini may have in fact been an illusion, not unlike the original act,” says Porter.
